correctness.rationale: A regular circumradius-one hexagon has exact norm N(u,v)=max(|u|+|v|/sqrt(3),2|v|/sqrt(3)). On a reduced angular interval, each of two displayed points simultaneously belongs to the radius-r hexagon translates about 0,e1,e2; the triangle-cover lemma covers half a fundamental square, and central reflection covers its complement. At the same points every lattice vector is at gauge distance at least r: the fourth corner is excluded by a support functional and all noncorner points are at Euclidean distance at least one while r<1. Exact linear-form substitutions show which witness applies on either side of the algebraically identified angle. Strict monotonicity and endpoint comparison yield complete equality classes. The embedded Python verifier ran successfully with 119356 diagnostics; finite checks are supporting evidence, not an infinite proof.
risks: Numerical verification only samples finitely many orientations, but the continuum theorem is established symbolically.

The 2026 motivating source treats minimal covering bodies and Minkowski-sum inequalities rather than this exact orientation optimization. Targeted semantic and web searches did not identify equivalent branch formulas; historical priority remains uncertain.

value.rationale: The object is a canonical rigid regular Euclidean hexagon relative to a canonical square lattice; orientation optimization is an independent natural geometric covering problem. The full continuum law identifies two genuinely competing critical holes and a nontrivial cusp at a strict symmetry-breaking optimal rotation, with unique minimizers modulo the known group actions. Exact bounds and equality classes are potentially useful test cases for anisotropic covering and lattice-hole geometry, and are not numerical recomputation of the previously known worst-rotation constant.
risks: The theorem does not address variable lattice, arbitrary centrally symmetric hexagons or higher dimensions.
